title: Explain Common Operating System Types and Their Purposes

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Operating systems connect users, applications, hardware, storage, and security. Recognize the major workstation and mobile systems, their filesystems, vendor life-cycle limits, and compatibility concerns.
The main mental model is: OS family → device purpose → filesystem → support life cycle → compatibility.
bullets: Workstation systems: Windows, Linux, macOS, and Chrome OS
Mobile systems: iPadOS, iOS, and Android
Filesystems: NTFS, ReFS, FAT32, ext4, XFS, APFS, and exFAT
sections.callout: Identify the device and workload, then match the OS, storage format, support status, and compatibility requirements.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes a device, application, filesystem, or support limitation, can you identify the operating system or compatibility issue involved?

entries.title: Windows
paragraphs: Microsoft Windows is widely used on business and consumer computers. Its broad application, hardware, driver, and enterprise-management support makes it a common workstation platform.
entries.recognitionCue: A standard business desktop needs common commercial applications and domain services → Windows.

entries.title: Linux
paragraphs: Linux is an open-source family of operating systems distributed in many versions. It is common on servers, development systems, embedded devices, and technical workstations.
entries.recognitionCue: A system emphasizes open-source tools, customization, or server administration → Linux.

entries.title: macOS
paragraphs: macOS is Apple's desktop operating system for Mac hardware. It integrates closely with Apple hardware, services, and the wider Apple ecosystem.
entries.recognitionCue: The workstation is a Mac → macOS.

entries.title: Chrome OS
paragraphs: Chrome OS is Google's lightweight, browser-centered operating system commonly found on Chromebooks. It emphasizes web applications, cloud services, and simple administration.
entries.memoryHook: Chrome OS = browser and cloud first.
entries.recognitionCue: A managed Chromebook relies primarily on web applications → Chrome OS.

table.caption: Workstation operating-system recognition
rows: Broad commercial hardware and application support

entries.title: iPadOS
paragraphs: iPadOS is Apple's operating system for iPad tablets, optimized for touch, larger tablet displays, multitasking, and supported accessories.
entries.recognitionCue: The device is an iPad → iPadOS.

entries.title: iOS
paragraphs: iOS is Apple's mobile operating system for iPhones. It is tightly controlled by Apple and integrates with Apple services and devices.
entries.recognitionCue: The device is an Apple smartphone → iOS.

entries.title: Android
paragraphs: Android is Google's mobile operating system used by many manufacturers across phones, tablets, and other devices. Vendor customization creates differences in interfaces and update schedules.
entries.memoryHook: Android = many vendors and form factors.
entries.recognitionCue: A non-Apple mobile device from one of many manufacturers → Android.

sections.title: Various Filesystem Types
paragraphs: A filesystem defines how an operating system organizes, stores, names, and retrieves files. Compatibility matters because an operating system may not natively read or write every filesystem.
sections.callout: Choose a filesystem for the operating system, device, required features, and cross-platform needs.

entries.title: New Technology File System (NTFS)
paragraphs: NTFS is the standard modern Windows filesystem. It supports permissions, journaling, large files, compression, and encryption-related features.
entries.recognitionCue: A Windows internal drive needs permissions and journaling → NTFS.

entries.title: Resilient File System (ReFS)
paragraphs: ReFS is a Microsoft filesystem designed for resilience, integrity, and large-scale storage scenarios rather than ordinary Windows boot volumes.
entries.recognitionCue: Storage integrity and resilience at scale → ReFS.

entries.title: File Allocation Table 32 (FAT32)
paragraphs: FAT32 is an older, widely compatible filesystem. Its key limitation is a maximum individual file size of about 4 GB.
entries.memoryHook: FAT32 = broad compatibility with a 4 GB file limit.
entries.recognitionCue: A removable drive cannot accept a file larger than 4 GB → FAT32 limitation.

entries.title: Fourth Extended Filesystem (ext4)
paragraphs: ext4 is a common general-purpose Linux filesystem with journaling, reliability, and broad Linux support.
entries.recognitionCue: A standard Linux installation needs a familiar local filesystem → ext4.

entries.title: Extended Filesystem (XFS)
paragraphs: XFS is a high-performance journaling filesystem used on Linux, especially for large files and scalable storage workloads.
entries.recognitionCue: A Linux workload emphasizes large files and scalable performance → XFS.

entries.title: Apple File System (APFS)
paragraphs: APFS is Apple's modern filesystem for macOS, iOS, and iPadOS. It is optimized for flash storage and supports encryption and snapshots.
entries.recognitionCue: A modern Mac or Apple mobile device uses its native filesystem → APFS.

entries.title: Extensible File Allocation Table (exFAT)
paragraphs: exFAT is designed for flash and removable storage, supports files larger than FAT32's limit, and is broadly compatible across modern operating systems.
entries.memoryHook: exFAT = portable sharing without FAT32's 4 GB limit.
entries.recognitionCue: A large file must move between Windows and macOS → exFAT.

sections.title: Vendor Life-Cycle Limitations

entries.title: End-of-Life (EOL)
paragraphs: End-of-life means the vendor has ended support for a product or version. Security fixes, compatibility updates, and technical assistance may stop.
entries.recognitionCue: An OS no longer receives vendor security updates → EOL.

entries.title: Update Limitations
paragraphs: A device may keep working but be unable to install newer OS or application updates because of unsupported hardware, storage limits, vendor policy, or an obsolete OS version.
entries.memoryHook: Update limitation = the device cannot move forward.
entries.recognitionCue: Hardware cannot support the next release → update limitation.

sections.callout: EOL describes vendor support status; an update limitation explains why a system cannot advance.

sections.title: Compatibility Concerns Between Operating Systems
paragraphs: Moving data, applications, or hardware between operating systems can expose compatibility problems. Verify support before migration or deployment.
bullets: Application compatibility: software for one platform may not run natively on another.
Driver compatibility: hardware needs a driver for the target OS and version.
Filesystem compatibility: another OS may read but not write a format, or not recognize it.
Feature compatibility: permissions, metadata, filenames, and formatting may not transfer exactly.
Peripheral and service compatibility: management, authentication, and device features can differ.
sections.callout: The same file, application, or device is not automatically portable across operating systems.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: System cannot install a newer release → update limitation

entries.title: FAT32 vs. exFAT
paragraphs: FAT32 has broad legacy compatibility but an approximately 4 GB file limit. exFAT supports larger files and modern cross-platform use.

entries.title: NTFS vs. exFAT
paragraphs: NTFS supplies Windows permissions and journaling. exFAT favors portable exchange.

entries.title: ext4 vs. XFS
paragraphs: ext4 is a common general-purpose Linux choice; XFS is associated with scalable, high-performance storage and large files.

entries.title: EOL vs. Update Limitation
paragraphs: EOL means vendor support has ended. An update limitation means a particular device cannot install a newer release.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: FAT32 → legacy compatibility, 4 GB file limit
Cross-platform move → verify applications, drivers, filesystems, and features
